article:
In a pub

Vibe coding is talking a product into existence with a model — here, Grok — and shipping the result before you understand every line. You describe what you want. You look at what comes back. You say what is wrong. You put it on the internet. That loop is the skill.

It is not a personality. It is not “I do not read errors.” It is not a replacement for judgement. The code still has to run. Money still has to move. A domain still has to point somewhere.

What it is not

It is not a computer science degree in a weekend. It is not collecting twenty tools. It is not waiting until the prompt is perfect. And it is not pretending the model cannot lie to you about what it just built.

If you only ever accept the first answer, you are not vibe coding. You are pasting.

What you should be able to do after this chapter

Open Grok. Describe a tiny thing a stranger could click. Get a first version. Know the difference between “it answered” and “it is live.”

That is the whole chapter. The next nineteen are the rest of the job: folders, GitHub, hosting, domains, secrets, memory, money, people.

How I actually do it

Almost everything on the Build list started as a conversation. Billboard was “one face, rising price, worlds behind it.” Scratchbox was “screenshots should not live on the Desktop.” Send Reorder was “the usual order, when the account goes quiet.” Meeting Mode was “a ritual for a call, optional Grok listening.”

I do not start with a stack. I start with a sentence a tired person would understand. Then I let Grok write the first files. Then I look. Then I argue. Then I deploy. The arguing is the work.

When something must remember state, take a pound, or sit in the Mac menu bar, I stop “forgetting the code exists.” I read the red text. I paste it back. I do not pretend I invented Swift.

Where noobs get stuck

They treat the chat as the product. A good answer in Grok is not a website. A zip of files on the Desktop is not shipped. Shipped means a URL that works when you close the laptop.

The other trap is shame. People wait to be invited. They wait to feel like a developer. Nobody is coming. The model will write the boring parts. You still have to point at a thing and say “this, live, today.”

Film this

Screen: a blank Grok chat. Say one sentence. Show the first files. Show the thing running. Then say the line out loud: the chat is not the product.

Do this before chapter 02

  • Open Grok and describe one tiny product in a single sentence.
  • Ask for the smallest version that can run in a browser.
  • Change one thing on purpose. See if it follows.
  • When it breaks, paste the error back. Do not start a new chat yet.
  • Write down what you still cannot do: host, domain, money. That list is the spine.

Next: models — what they can do, what they cannot, and which one for which job. You do not need five. You need one you will actually talk to.
